LORD God
LAWRD GAWD
compound divine title
A translation of the Hebrew compound YHWH Elohim (יהוה אלהים) — the personal covenant name of God (the Tetragrammaton, rendered LORD in small capitals) joined to the generic title Elohim (God, the Creator of Genesis 1). The Authorized Version and virtually all English translations render the compound as “LORD God,” with small-capital LORD signaling the Tetragrammaton and plain-type God rendering Elohim. This title appears first in Genesis 2:4 at the hinge between the cosmic creation narrative (Gen 1:1–2:3) and the Garden narrative (Gen 2:4ff.), signaling the unity of Creator and Covenant-Lord.

Biblical Definition

The compound title “LORD God” (YHWH Elohim) unites the two most theologically freighted divine names in the Old Testament. Elohim is the transcendent Creator who speaks the cosmos into existence in Genesis 1, a title emphasizing power, plurality-of-majesty, and cosmic sovereignty. YHWH is the covenant God who enters into personal relationship with His people, speaks face-to-face, redeems from bondage, and binds Himself to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob by sworn oath.

The first appearance of the compound (Gen 2:4) is the Scriptures' declaration that these are not two gods but one: the transcendent Maker of heaven and earth is the same personal Redeemer who forms man from the dust and breathes life into him. When the serpent speaks in Genesis 3, he notably uses Elohim alone (Gen 3:1: “Hath God said?”), subtly severing the covenant relationship from the created order — as if the Creator were merely an impersonal force whose commands were debatable.

The compound title recurs throughout the historical and prophetic books at moments of covenant affirmation. Amos 4:13 — “The LORD God of hosts is His name” — grounds the judgment oracle in the identity of the One who both created and covenants. Revelation's climactic vision collapses the temple into the presence of “And I saw no temple therein: for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it.” (Rev 21:22) — Creator and Redeemer as one, the compound title reaching its eschatological fulfillment. Classical Reformed theology insists that the unity of the divine names is not merely grammatical but ontological: the God who creates and the God who saves are identical.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) treats LORD and God as separate entries, but notes the compounded title: LORD God in Scripture typically renders the Hebrew Adonai Elohim (when spoken aloud) or YHWH Elohim (in the consonantal text), the two great divine names joined to declare that the transcendent Creator is the covenant-keeping personal God of Israel.

LORD GOD — in the English Bible, this compound renders YHWH Elohim: YHWH (the Tetragrammaton, God's personal covenant name) + Elohim (the generic title for the divine Being as Creator); first appearing at the hinge of Genesis 2:4, the compound declares the unity of the transcendent Creator-God and the covenant-LORD who enters human history.

The theological significance of the compound is anti-Gnostic and anti-Marcionite: the God who made the world and the God who redeems from sin are the same God; there is no lower Demiurge who created matter and a higher spiritual redeemer above him; one LORD God is Creator, Lawgiver, and Savior.

In the prophetic corpus, “thus says the LORD God” (Hebrew kō ’āmar YHWH Elohim) is the prophetic messenger formula par excellence — an assertion that the word being delivered originates with the One who both made the cosmos and entered covenant with Israel, binding both creation and history to His sovereign purpose.

Key Scripture

Gen 2:4 — "These are the generations of the heavens and of the earth when they were created, in the day that the LORD God made the earth and the heavens,"

Gen 3:1 — "Now the serpent was more subtil than any beast of the field which the LORD God had made. And he said unto the woman, Yea, hath God said, Ye shall not eat of every tree of the garden?"

Amos 4:13 — "For, lo, he that formeth the mountains, and createth the wind, and declareth unto man what is his thought, that maketh the morning darkness, and treadeth upon the high places of the earth, The LORD, The God of hosts, is his name."

Rev 21:22 — "And I saw no temple therein: for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it."

Modern Corruption

Gnostic and Marcionite traditions ancient and modern drive a wedge between the Creator-God and the Redeemer-God; contemporary Open Theism re-opens the wound from the opposite direction, assigning to “God” a limited foreknowledge that undermines the LORD's covenant sovereignty.

expand to see more

The oldest corruption of the compound “LORD God” is the Gnostic and Marcionite severing of Creator from Redeemer. Marcion (c. 144 AD) taught that the wrathful Creator-God of the Old Testament was a different, inferior deity from the loving Father revealed by Jesus. The compound title YHWH Elohim is the Scripture's own refutation of this heresy: the God who made the world (Elohim, Gen 1) is the same God who enters covenant (YHWH, Gen 2), judges sin (Gen 3), and redeems His people (Exod 3). The Nicene and Apostles' Creeds both declare that the Father is the Maker of heaven and earth, identifying the Creator explicitly with the God of the gospel — a direct anti-Marcionite confession. Modern versions of the error reappear in progressive theologies that portray the OT God as violent and tribal while the NT God is loving and inclusive; this is Marcionism with political cosmetics.

Open Theism (Clark Pinnock, Gregory Boyd) represents a second corruption from the Reformed perspective: it retains the unity of Creator and Redeemer but empties the covenant title YHWH of its eternal foreknowledge content. If God does not exhaustively know the future, then “the LORD God” who promised Abraham a seed and Moses deliverance was making commitments on the basis of limited information — a theological absurdity. Amos 4:13 grounds God's knowledge of human thought in His creative sovereignty: the One who forms mountains and creates the wind also “declares to man what his thought is.” The compound title demands a God who is both omnipotent Creator and omniscient Covenant-Lord.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The compound divine title roots covenant theology in creation theology, insisting that the redeeming God of Exodus is the same as the making God of Genesis, and that the eschatological fulfillment of Revelation consummates both creation and covenant simultaneously.

expand to see more

Hebrew Tetragrammaton YHWH (יהוה) — the unspeakable personal name of God, traditionally vocalized Yahweh or Jehovah; it encodes God's eternal self-existence (Exod 3:14: “I AM THAT I AM”) and His covenant faithfulness to the patriarchs

Hebrew Elohim (אלהים) — the plural-of-majesty form of El or Eloah, used for the transcendent Creator of Genesis 1; the plural does not indicate polytheism but the fullness and majesty of the singular divine Being; used with singular verbs to emphasize that the many attributes of God belong to one Person

Genesis 2:4 — the structural hinge of the creation narrative, shifting from the cosmic (Gen 1:1–2:3, Elohim) to the relational (Gen 2:4ff., YHWH Elohim); the compound at the seam declares that the God of covenant is identical with the God of creation, anticipating the Nicene declaration that the Father is both Maker and Source of redemption

Genesis 3:1 — the serpent's tactical use of “God” (Elohim) alone rather than “LORD God” (YHWH Elohim), severing the covenant relationship from the created order; Eve's response (Gen 3:3) mirrors this, using “God” for the One who forbade the tree, as if the covenant-LORD's personal prohibition had become an impersonal rule

Rev 21:22 — the eschatological arrival of the compound title's fullness: “the Lord God, the Almighty, and the Lamb” replace the temple because they are the temple; Creator, Covenant-LORD, and the Lamb-Redeemer are one presence, the compound title's promise fulfilled in the new creation

Usage

"The Shema (Deut 6:4) — “The LORD our God, the LORD is one” — functions as the daily covenant confession that the two divine titles belong to one undivided God; Jewish tradition regarded this as the supreme assertion of monotheism against the polytheism of the surrounding nations."

"Athanasius' On the Incarnation grounds the Son's redemptive work in the Father's creative word: if the Creator's image-bearing creature fell into corruption, the Creator Himself must restore what He originally made; the compound title YHWH Elohim underlies this Athanasian logic of redemption-as-recreation."

"The prophetic messenger formula “Thus says the LORD God” (kō ’āmar YHWH Elohim) appears dozens of times in Ezekiel alone, grounding each oracular word in the full authority of the God who is both Creator and Covenant-LORD, so that to reject the prophet's word is to reject both the Maker of all things and the Redeemer of Israel."
